rounds.proof_sketch: Thread tid=160 reaches i=4000 since 4000 ≡ 160 (mod 256). This causes out-of-bounds write to shared[4000]. However, the output store loop uses 'i < cols' (not mutated), so only shared[0:3999] are read back. The corrupted shared[4000] never affects the output.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the load loop from 'i < cols' to 'i <= cols', causing thread 160 to execute one extra iteration where i=4000. This writes an out-of-bounds read value to shared[4000]. However, the critical observation is that the store loop on line 83 still uses 'i < cols', meaning the output is constructed only from shared[0:3999]. The infected memory location shared[4000] is never read during output generation. Therefore, while the mutation causes different memory accesses, the observable output remains identical for all possible input values.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed shape [128, 4000]. The mutation's effect (corrupting shared[4000]) does not propagate to output because the store loop bounds prevent reading from corrupted location. Would require either: (1) cols divisible by blockDim.x to cause different aliasing, or (2) mutating the store loop as well.
rounds.recommendations: When mutating loop bounds in kernels with separate load/store phases, ensure mutations are applied consistently to both loops if testing for behavioral differences. Also consider that out-of-bounds writes may not propagate if they land outside the region used for output computation.
